q: As per ASTM standards, materials passing through a 19 mm (3/4 inch) sieve and retained on a 4.75 mm (No. 4) sieve are classified as?
n: Under ASTM D2487 (USCS), gravel passing the 19 mm sieve and retained on the 4.75 mm (No. 4) sieve is fine gravel. Coarse gravel is 75–19 mm. Source: ASTM D2487 (Unified Soil Classification System).

q: As per AASHTO standards, materials passing a 0.425 mm (No. 40) sieve and retained on a 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve are classified as?
n: AASHTO M 145 defines fine sand as particles passing the 0.425 mm (No. 40) sieve and retained on the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve. Source: AASHTO M 145 (soil classification).

q: Which term refers to the portion of a building located above ground level. including all structural and architectural components?
n: The superstructure is the part of a building above ground level. The substructure (foundations) is below. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: A reinforced concrete beam is intentionally constructed with a slight upward curvature before any service loads are applied. This upward curvature is provided to offset anticipated downward deflection and improve the beam's final appearance and performance under load. What is this feature called?
n: Camber is a slight upward curvature built into a beam to offset expected deflection under load. Source: ACI 318 / NSCP 2015, deflection provisions; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Also known as Young's Modulus, it shows the stiffness of a material to resist axial deformation and is the ratio of longitudinal stress to the longitudinal strain.
n: Young's modulus (modulus of elasticity) is the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain. It measures stiffness against axial deformation. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 3.

q: It is a measure of how susceptible a column or compression member is to buckling under axial load. It describes the relationship between the member's length and its cross-sectional stiffness.
n: Slenderness ratio (KL/r) relates a compression member's effective length to its radius of gyration. It indicates how susceptible the member is to buckling. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 13 (Buckling of Columns).

q: Also known as flexure, it is a phenomenon that occurs when a structural element is subjected to load applied perpendicularly to a longitudinal axis of the element.
n: Bending (flexure) occurs when a member is loaded perpendicular to its longitudinal axis. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 6 (Bending).

q: The deformation due to an applied load measured by the displacement of a point from its original position expressed in terms of distance or angle.
n: Deflection is the displacement of a point from its original position under load, expressed as a distance or an angle. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 12 (Deflection of Beams and Shafts).

q: Which fundamental structural parameter describes the internal force per unit area within a material, determining its ability to resist applied loads and influencing failure modes in engineering design?
n: Stress is internal force per unit area. It governs how a material resists loads and how it fails. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 1.

q: During a tensile test on a structural steel specimen, the engineer observes that the material begins to experience significant deformation without a corresponding increase in applied stress. Beyond this stage, the steel does not fully return to its original shape even after the load is removed. Which point on the stress-strain curve has most likely been reached?
o: Proportional Limit, because stress remains directly proportional to strain.
Fracture Point, because the specimen has completely lost its load-carrying capacity.
Ultimate Strength, because the maximum stress capacity of the material has already been attained.
Yield Point, because the material begins to undergo permanent deformation under nearly constant stress.
n: At the yield point, strain increases markedly at nearly constant stress, and the deformation is permanent once unloaded. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 3 (Stress–Strain Diagram).

q: During a tensile test of a structural steel specimen, the applied load continues to increase beyond the yield point until the specimen reaches its maximum load-carrying capacity. Beyond this stage, localized necking begins and the load that can be sustained by the specimen starts to decrease. Which point on the stress-strain curve has most likely been reached?
o: Proportional Limit, because stress and strain remain directly proportional within the elastic range.
Yield Point, because the material begins to experience permanent deformation without a significant increase in stress.
Ultimate Strength, because the specimen has reached its maximum stress capacity before the onset of necking and eventual fracture.
Fracture Point, because the material has completely lost its ability to resist the applied load.
n: Ultimate strength is the maximum stress the specimen can carry. After it, necking begins and the load falls until fracture. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 3 (Stress–Strain Diagram).

q: Which material functions as the primary binder in concrete, initiating hydration and chemically transforming the mixture into a cohesive, load-bearing structure?
n: Portland cement is the binder. It hydrates with water to form the paste that binds aggregates into a hard mass. Source: Kosmatka et al., Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (PCA), Ch. 2.

q: Which admixture is primarily responsible for reducing water content in a concrete mix while maintaining workability and flow ability without compromising strength?
n: Plasticizers (water reducers) cut the water needed for a given workability without losing strength. Source: ASTM C494 (Type A/F admixtures); PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, Ch. 6.

q: Which key properties of concrete are primarily affected by the water-cement ratio?
o: Reinforcement spacing, color, and surface texture
Aggregate size, slump value, and curing time
Formwork type, setting time, and bar diameter
n: The water–cement ratio mainly controls compressive strength, workability and durability. Lower w/c gives stronger, denser concrete. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (Abrams' law).

q: What is the best method of curing concrete so that it continues to gain strength?
o: By consistently using a concrete vibrator to evenly spread concrete
Do not remove formworks for the first 2 weeks of curing
Water curing regularly to delay shrinkage cracking
Do not apply heavy loads on the concrete surface while curing
n: Keeping concrete continuously moist (water curing) lets hydration continue and strength develop, and delays drying shrinkage cracking. Source: ACI 308R (Guide to Curing Concrete); NSCP 2015, Sec. 426.5.3.

q: What is the purpose of control joints for concrete slab on grade in construction?
o: To reduce steel reinforcement for cost efficiency
To plan cracks in a straight line
To allow for movements caused by temperature changes
To improve construction quality by segmenting concrete pouring
n: Control (contraction) joints are planned weakened planes, so shrinkage cracks form neatly along the joint rather than at random. Source: ACI 224.3R (Joints in Concrete Construction).

q: The point on a stress-strain curve that indicates the limit of elastic behavior and the beginning of plastic behavior. Beyond this point, deformation occurs permanently.
n: The elastic limit is the greatest stress at which the material still fully recovers its shape. Beyond it, deformation is permanent (plastic). Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 3.

q: Which mechanical property defines the maximum stress a material can withstand before it begins-to.deform plastically and no longer returns to its original shape?
n: Yield strength is the stress at which a material begins to deform plastically and will no longer return to its original shape. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 3.

q: Which among the following is a non-load-bearing wall?
n: A curtain wall is a non-load-bearing exterior wall hung from the structural frame. It carries only its own weight and wind loads. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (Curtain Walls).

q: According to NSCP 2015, what is the minimum number of vertical reinforcement bars required for a rectangular tied concrete column?
n: Rectangular or circular tied columns need at least four longitudinal bars. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 410.7.3.1.

q: According to NSCP 2015, what is the minimum number of vertical reinforcement bars required for a spiral concrete column?
n: Columns with spirals need at least six longitudinal bars. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 410.7.3.1.

q: Where anchor bolts are used to connect horizontal elements to the columns, anchor bolts shall be placed within lateral ties. Lateral ties shall enclose both the vertical bars in the column and the anchor bolts. There shall be a minimum of two 12 mm diameter lateral ties provided in the top ___ mm of the column.
n: Where anchor bolts are at the top of a column, at least two 12 mm ties must enclose the bars and bolts within the top 125 mm. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 425.7.2.3 (ACI 318-14, 25.7.2.3).

q: A developer intends to construct a high-rise office building requiring long spans, rapid erection, and reduced structural dead load. Which structural material would generally be MOST advantageous for the primary framing system?
o: Reinforced Concrete, because its inherent stiffness, durability, and fire resistance make it suitable for multi-storey construction.
Composite Steel-Concrete Construction, because combining structural steel and reinforced concrete can improve overall structural performance and economy.
Structural Steel, because its high strength-to-weight ratio allows longer spans, lighter framing, and faster construction.
Prestressed Concrete, because prestressing enables longer spans. improved crack control, and reduced member depth compared to conventional reinforced concrete.
n: Structural steel's high strength-to-weight ratio allows longer spans, lighter framing (less dead load) and faster erection. Source: Salmon & Johnson, Steel Structures: Design and Behavior, Ch. 1.

q: In a multi-storey steel building, beams must be connected to columns using standardized steel connectors that safely transfer shear and, when required, moment. Which of the following components is typically used to connect a beam to a column in modern multi-storey steel framing?
n: A shear tab (single plate) is the standard simple beam-to-column shear connection in multi-storey steel framing. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual (connection types), Part 10.

q: Steel beams connected usually by placing them on top of a steel angle that is attached to a column or girder, the purpose of which is to transfer loads from the beam to the supporting columns or girders as well as to provide stability.
n: A seated beam rests on a steel angle (seat) attached to the column or girder. The seat transfers the beam reaction and steadies the beam. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual (connection types), Part 10 (Seated Connections).

q: Steel beams that interlock and fit tightly via cuts and slots.
n: Coped beams have flanges and webs cut away so they fit tightly into the supporting member. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual (connection types), Part 9 (Coped Beams).

q: A type of connection for steel beams where it is connected to the supporting steel structure through a fitting
n: In a framed connection the beam web is fastened to the support through fittings such as double clip angles. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual (connection types), Part 10 (Framed Connections).

q: A secondary steel beam must frame into a much deeper girder while maintaining the same top-of-steel elevation. The top flange of the incoming beam would clash with the girder's flange unless part of the beam is cut away to allow proper fit-up and bolt access for the shear connection. Which type of beam end treatment is required in this situation?
n: Cutting away the top flange so the beam fits under the girder flange at the same top-of-steel elevation is coping. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual (connection types), Part 9 (Coped Beams).

q: A steel beam must be connected to a column flange in a typical multi-storey frame. The engineer wants a simple shear connection that allows rotation, uses a single plate welded to the column, and requires the beam to be bolted through its web; no bearing seat is needed. Which type of connection is being described?
n: A single plate welded to the column with the beam web bolted to it is a shear tab (single-plate) connection. It is a simple connection that allows rotation. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual (connection types), Part 10 (Single-Plate Connections).

q: A steel beam must be connected to the side of a supporting member in a situation where the contractor prefers a traditional shear connection made from two small components attached to the beam web. These components allow the beam to be fastened to the supporting member without requiring flange cuts or a bearing seat, and the system has been widely used for decades due to its simplicity and adaptability. Which connection is being described?
n: Two clip angles attached to the beam web form the traditional double-angle (clip angle) shear connection. It needs no flange cuts or seat. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual (connection types), Part 10 (Double-Angle Connections).

q: A steel beam must be supported in a location where erection access is limited and the contractor prefers a connection that allows the beam to be placed directly onto a small supporting component before final fastening. This method provides immediate bearing during installation and is commonly used when rapid placement or temporary self-support of the beam is desired. Which connection is being described?
n: A seated connection lets the beam rest on a seat angle before final fastening. It gives immediate bearing during erection. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual (connection types), Part 10 (Seated Connections).

q: A steel W-section beam is subjected to unusually high shear demand near the support due to a heavy point load. Analysis shows that the web is too thin and is at risk of local web buckling. The engineer instructs that additional steel plates be welded directly onto the web. In steel design practice, what is the purpose of these added plates?
o: To transfer composite action between steel and concrete through shear studs
To strengthen the web against shear by acting as web doublers that prevent web buckling
To increase the beam's flexural capacity by enlarging the compression flange
To reduce lateral-torsional buckling by stiffening the compression flange
n: Plates welded to a thin web are web doubler plates. They raise the web's shear strength and prevent local web buckling. Source: AISC 360-16, Sec. J10.6 (Web Panel-Zone Shear) and Sec. G (doubler plates).

q: A beam supporting other smaller beams and serves as the main horizontal supports of a structure.
n: A girder is a large main beam that supports other, smaller beams. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: A beam whose both ends are rigidly fixed into the supports
n: A fixed (built-in) beam has both ends rigidly fixed against rotation. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 12 (Statically Indeterminate Beams).

q: A reinforced concrete beam is rigidly restrained against rotation at both supports. Compared with a simply supported beam of the same span and loading, what is the MOST significant structural advantage of this support condition?
o: The beam develops negative moments at the supports, reducing the maximum positive moment and deflection within the span.
The beam behaves as a tension member at the supports, allowing a reduction in longitudinal reinforcement.
The beam eliminates shear stresses near the supports because end fixity transfers all loads through bending action.
The beam transfers all loads directly to the supports without developing flexural stresses along its length.
n: End fixity creates negative moments at the supports. These cut the maximum positive moment (wL²/24 at midspan versus wL²/8) and the deflection. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 12; AISC Manual, Beam Diagrams and Formulas.

q: What do you call a beam that is supported at both ends and also at one or more intermediate supports along its span?
n: A continuous beam rests on more than two supports: both ends plus one or more intermediate supports. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 12.

q: In a simply supported beam under normal loading conditions, at which part of the beam does positive bending moment develop?
n: In a simply supported beam under gravity load, positive (sagging) moment develops along the span and peaks at midspan. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 6.

q: In a simply supported beam, where does the negative bending moment develop?
n: A simply supported beam under gravity load has no negative moment. Moment is zero at the supports and positive throughout the span. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 6.

q: A simply supported reinforced concrete beam is subjected to a uniform load from slab and partition walls. During serviceability evaluation, the engineer notes that the region experiencing the greatest curvature corresponds to the location of maximum bending moment. At which part of the beam is excessive vertical displacement MOST likely to occur?
o: At the compression zone near the top fibers
n: With a uniform load, maximum moment and curvature, and therefore maximum deflection (5wL⁴/384EI), occur at midspan. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 12.

q: A projecting beam fixed only at one end while the other end has no support
n: A cantilever is fixed at one end and free at the other. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 6.

q: A projecting reinforced concrete balcony is rigidly connected to a building at one end and unsupported at the other. Under gravity loads, where is the tensile stress greatest?
o: At the bottom fibers near the fixed support because positive bending develops adjacent to the support.
At the top fibers near the fixed support because negative bending moment is greatest at the support.
At the neutral axis near midspan because internal stresses concentrate at the geometric center of the member.
At the bottom fibers near the free end because deflection is greatest at that location.
n: A cantilever has its largest (negative) moment at the fixed support. Tension is therefore greatest in the top fibers there, which is why the main bars go at the top. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 6; NSCP 2015, Sec. 409 (flexural reinforcement).

q: A horizontal structural element constructed along the external wall of the building, also referred to as an edge beam.
n: A spandrel beam runs along the exterior wall at the edge of each floor. It is also called an edge beam. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: A beam that extends beyond the wall or column support
n: An overhanging beam extends past one or both of its wall or column supports. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 6.

q: What is a beam, either below or above ground, used for connecting two structural members to keep them from spreading apart?
n: A tie beam connects two structural members, such as footings or column bases, to keep them from spreading apart. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.
